'''Dame Fiona Margaret Powrie''' {{post-nominals|country=GBR|size=100%|DBE|FRS|FMedSci}} (born 1963) is currently the head of the Kennedy Institute of Rheumatology at the [[University of Oxford]].<ref>{{Cite book|title=Powrie, Prof. Fiona Margaret {{!}} WHO'S WHO & WHO WAS WHO|year=2012|language=en|doi=10.1093/ww/9780199540884.013.255684|chapter = Powrie, Prof. Fiona Margaret, (born 1963), Director, Kennedy Institute of Rheumatology and Professor, Nuffield Department of Orthopaedics, Rheumatology and Muskuloskeletal Sciences, University of Oxford, since 2014; Fellow of Wadham College, Oxford, since 2014}}</ref> Formerly she was the inaugural Sidney Truelove Professor of Gastroenterology at the [[University of Oxford]]. She is also head of the Experimental Medicine Division of the Nuffield Department of Clinical Medicine.<ref name="Ndm.ox.ac.uk">{{cite web |url=http://www.ndm.ox.ac.uk/principal-investigators/researcher/fiona-powrie |title=Nuffield Department of Clinical Medicine – Prof Fiona Powrie FRS |publisher=Ndm.ox.ac.uk |access-date=2012-11-15 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121120132957/http://www.ndm.ox.ac.uk/principal-investigators/researcher/fiona-powrie |archive-date=20 November 2012 |url-status=dead }}</ref>

==Career==
Powrie studied biochemistry at the [[University of Bath]],<ref>{{cite web |url=http://2012.the-embo-meeting.org/programme/keynotes-a-plenaries/keynotes.html |title=Keynotes |publisher=2012.the-embo-meeting.org |access-date=2012-11-15 |archive-date=24 June 2013 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130624202557/http://2012.the-embo-meeting.org/programme/keynotes-a-plenaries/keynotes.html |url-status=dead }}</ref> before completing a [[Doctor of Philosophy|DPhil]] degree in [[Professor Don Mason|Don Mason's]] lab at the [[Sir William Dunn School of Pathology]], the [[University of Oxford]].<ref name="wordpress1">{{cite web |url=http://wellcometrust.wordpress.com/2012/01/31/a-delicate-balance-intestinal-inflammation/ |title=A delicate balance: Investigating intestinal inflammation « Wellcome Trust Blog |publisher=Wellcometrust.wordpress.com |date=2012-01-31 |access-date=2012-11-15 }}{{Dead link|date=August 2025 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }}</ref>

==Notable work==
===Regulatory T cells===
Powrie worked with [[Don Mason (immunologist)|Don Mason]] at the [[Sir William Dunn School of Pathology]] studying the interactions of different subsets of [[T helper cells|CD4+ T cells]] in rats. This work identified that CD4+OX22hi (OX22 is CD45RC in rats and the equivalent of CD45RB in mice, both [[isoforms]] of [[CD45]]<ref>{{cite journal|vauthors=Saouid A, Seddon B, Heath V, Fowell D, Mason D |year=1996|title= The physiological role of regulatory T cells in the prevention of autoimmunity: the function of the thymus in the generation of the regulatory T cell subset|journal= Immunological Reviews |pmid=9005215|volume=149|pages=195–216|doi=10.1111/j.1600-065x.1996.tb00905.x|s2cid=40160832}}</ref>) T cells contained pathogenic activity while [[CD4]]+OX22lo T cells contained regulatory activity and could prevent the pathogenic activity of CD4+OX22hi T cells<ref>{{cite journal|vauthors=Powrie F, Mason D |year=1990|title= OX-22high CD4+ T cells induce wasting disease with multiple organ pathology: prevention by the OX-22low subset|journal= Journal of Experimental Medicine |pmid=2258700|pmc=2188779|volume=172|issue=6|pages=1701–8|doi=10.1084/jem.172.6.1701}}</ref> These were foundational studies and represented some of the seminal work on [[regulatory T cell]]s (Treg).

===Intestinal inflammation===
Powrie performed post-doctoral studies with Robert L. Coffman at DNAX in Palo Alto, California. Here, she extended her earlier work in rats to mice and developed the "T cell transfer" model, one of the most prominent models of intestinal inflammation where transfer of CD4+CD45RBhi T cells to [[Recombination activating gene|Rag]] deficient or [[Severe combined immunodeficiency|SCID]] mice led to the development of severe intestinal inflammation and wasting disease. This could be prevented by transfer of CD4+CD45RBlo T cells.<ref>{{cite journal|vauthors=Powrie F, Leach MW, Mauze S, Caddle LB, Coffman RL |year=1993|title= Phenotypically distinct subsets of CD4+ T cells induce or protect from chronic intestinal inflammation in C. B-17 scid mice |journal=[[International Immunology]]|pmid=7903159|volume=5|issue=11|pages=1461–71|doi=10.1093/intimm/5.11.1461}}</ref> Using this model Powrie further identified the pathogenic role played by [[interferon-gamma|IFN-γ]] and [[tumour necrosis factor-alpha|TNF-α]] in intestinal inflammation and the therapeutic potential of [[Interleukin-10|IL-10]]<ref>{{cite journal|vauthors=Powrie F, Leach MW, Mauze S, Menon S, Caddle LB, Coffman RL |year=1994|title=Inhibition of Th1 responses prevents inflammatory bowel disease in scid mice reconstituted with CD45RBhi CD4+ T cells|journal=Immunity|pmid=7600284|volume=1|issue=7|pages=553–62|doi=10.1016/1074-7613(94)90045-0}}</ref> and highlighted the requirement for [[Transforming growth factor beta|TGF-β]] in the prevention of colitis by the CD4+CD45RBlo regulatory T cell subset<ref>{{cite journal|vauthors=Powrie F, Carlino J, Leach MW, Mauze S, Coffman RL |title=A critical role for transforming growth factor-beta but not interleukin 4 in the suppression of T helper type 1-mediated colitis by CD45RB(low) CD4+ T cells |year=1996|journal=Journal of Experimental Medicine|pmid=8676088|volume=183|issue=6|pmc=2192626|pages=2669–74|doi=10.1084/jem.183.6.2669}}</ref>
Upon returning to the University of Oxford in 1996, first to the Nuffield Department of Surgery and later, the Sir William Dunn School of Pathology, Powrie used the T cell transfer model to identify the suppressive mechanisms used by regulatory T cells to prevent intestinal inflammation including the requirements for [[CTLA-4]]<ref>{{cite journal|vauthors=Read S, Malmstrom V, Powrie F |title=Cytotoxic T lymphocyte-associated antigen 4 plays an essential role in the function of CD25(+)CD4(+) regulatory cells that control intestinal inflammation |year=2000|journal=Journal of Experimental Medicine|pmid=10899916|volume=192|issue=2|pmc=2193261|pages=295–302|doi=10.1084/jem.192.2.295}}</ref> and the capacity of Treg to prevent colitis driven by innate immune cells as well as CD4+ T cells.<ref>{{cite journal|vauthors=Maloy KJ, Salaun L, Cahill R, Dougan G, Saunders NJ, Powrie F |title=CD4+CD25+ T(R) cells suppress innate immune pathology through cytokine-dependent mechanisms |year=2003|journal=Journal of Experimental Medicine|pmid=12515818|volume=197|issue=1|pmc=2193798|pages=111–9|doi=10.1084/jem.20021345}}</ref> Focusing on pathogenic mechanisms the Powrie lab. identified the critical role played by the cytokine IL-23 in driving pathology in the intestine<ref>{{cite journal|vauthors=Hue S, Ahern P, Buonocore S, Kullberg MC, Cua DJ, McKenzie BS, Powrie F, Maloy KJ |title=Interleukin-23 drives innate and T cell-mediated intestinal inflammation|year=2006|journal=Journal of Experimental Medicine|pmid=17030949|doi=10.1084/jem.20061099|volume=203|issue=11|pmc=2118132|pages=2473–83}}</ref>

===Therapeutic potential of Tregs===
Work from the Powrie lab. identified that Treg could not alone prevent inflammatory bowel disease but could actually cure established inflammation.<ref>{{cite journal|vauthors=Mottet C, Uhlig HH, Powrie F |title=Cutting edge: cure of colitis by CD4+CD25+ regulatory T cells|year=2003|journal=Journal of Immunology |pmid=12682220|volume=170|issue=8|pages=3939–43|doi=10.4049/jimmunol.170.8.3939|doi-access=free}}</ref> Furthermore, Powrie was among the first to identify a population of CD4+CD25+ T cells in human peripheral blood that possessed regulatory capacity, confirming these cells as a bona fide T cell subset in humans.<ref>{{cite journal|vauthors=Stephens LA, Mottet C, Mason D, Powrie F |title=Human CD4(+)CD25(+) thymocytes and peripheral T cells have immune suppressive activity in vitro|year=2001|journal=European Journal of Immunology |pmid=11298351|doi=10.1002/1521-4141(200104)31:4<1247::AID-IMMU1247>3.0.CO;2-M|volume=31|issue=4|pages=1247–54|doi-access=free}}</ref>

==Honours and awards==
In 2009, Powrie was appointed as the inaugural Sidney Truelove Professor of Gastroenterology within the Nuffield Department of Clinical Medicine in Oxford.<ref name="Ndm.ox.ac.uk"/> She was elected a Fellow of the [[Royal Society]] in 2011,<ref>{{cite web|url=http://royalsociety.org/people/fiona-powrie/ |title=Professor Fiona Margaret Powrie FRS |publisher=Royal Society |access-date=2012-11-15}}</ref> and was awarded the [[Louis-Jeantet Prize for Medicine]] in 2012.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.eurekalert.org/pub_releases/2012-01/embo-2lp012512.php |title=2012 Louis-Jeantet Prize for Medicine |publisher=Eurekalert.org |access-date=2012-11-15}}</ref> In 2014, she was elected a Fellow of the [[Academy of Medical Sciences (United Kingdom)|Academy of Medical Sciences]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Professor Dame Fiona Powrie DBE FRS FMedSci |url=https://acmedsci.ac.uk/fellows/fellows-directory/ordinary-fellows/fellow/Fiona%20Margaret-Powrie-0033z00002qIIlkAAG |access-date=2026-06-02 |website=Academy of Medical Sciences}}</ref>

The [[University of Bath]] awarded Powrie an [[Honorary Doctorate]] of Science in June 2015.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Professor Fiona Powrie: oration |url=https://www.bath.ac.uk/corporate-information/professor-fiona-powrie-oration/ |access-date=2025-10-09 |website=www.bath.ac.uk}}</ref>

Powrie was appointed [[Dame Commander of the Order of the British Empire]] (DBE) in the [[2022 Birthday Honours]] for services to medical science.<ref>{{London Gazette|issue=63714|supp=y|page=B9|date=1 June 2022}}</ref>
